I'm 60 years old this year, and I've been farming in Quzhou for over 40 years. Finishing senior high school back in my day meant I was one of the few educated young men in the village, and over the decades I've tried to farm with my head as much as my hands. I read the extension bulletins when they come around, I keep notes on what works, and I calculate my fertilizer in kilograms per mu rather than just counting bags like some of my neighbors.

This year I'm keeping my 12 mu much the same as last year: 10 mu in wheat-maize double cropping and 2 mu of cotton. The wheat went in last October after rotary tillage, using an improved Shimai variety. Now that it's greening up, I'm planning my spring inputs carefully. Based on soil conditions and the county extension recommendations, I'm targeting 18 kg of nitrogen per mu — about 12 kg as basal compound and another 6 kg of urea topdressed at jointing — plus 6 kg of phosphorus and 4 kg of potassium per mu as compound. The wheat needs four irrigations total: one winter irrigation I already did, and three more in spring at green-up, jointing, and grain filling. With decent weather I expect 500 kg per mu.

For summer maize, I'll plant hybrid seed — probably Nongda 372 from the seed station — immediately after wheat harvest in early June. There's no time for tillage between crops, so it'll be no-tillage direct seeding. I'll apply 16 kg N per mu, mostly as side-dress at the big trumpet stage, plus 4 kg P and 3 kg K as basal compound. Two irrigations should be enough, one at jointing and one at filling, and I should get about 550 kg per mu.

I'm keeping 2 mu of cotton because the lint price has been stable, but at 60 I can't manage much more — the hand-picking and pruning are hard on my back. I'll use an improved Guoxinmian variety, rotary till in late April, and apply 14 kg N, 6 kg P, and 5 kg K per mu. Cotton is pesticide-intensive here; I'll need about 14 sprayings for bollworms, aphids, and weeds. I expect around 250 kg per mu of seed cotton. Some neighbors are switching to vegetables, but I don't trust the price volatility. Wheat-maize gives me grain I can always sell or eat, and cotton provides cash. That's my balance.
